chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban, who said:

Al-Ahwal informed me that Zayd ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn (peace be upon him) sent for him while he was in concealment. He said: So I went to him and he said to me, 'O Abu Ja'far! What do you say — if a comer from among us comes to you, would you go out with him?' So I said to him, 'If it were your father or your uncle, I would go out with him.' He said, 'I intend to go out and fight these people, so come out with me.' I said, 'No, I would not do so, may I be your ransom.'

He said, 'Are you placing your own self above mine?' I said to him, 'It is but one soul. If there is a Divine Authority (Hujja) for God on earth, then the one who stays behind from you is saved and the one who goes out with you is destroyed. And if there is no Divine Authority for God on earth, then the one who stays behind from you and the one who goes out with you are equal.'

He said, 'O Abu Ja'far! I used to sit with my father at the dining table, and he would feed me the choicest morsels and cool the hot food for me until it cooled, out of compassion for me — yet he did not protect me from the heat of the Fire by informing you of the Religion and not informing me of it?'

I said to him, 'May I be your ransom! It was out of his compassion for you from the heat of the Fire that he did not inform you — he feared for you lest you not accept it and thus enter the Fire. But he informed me: if I accept, I am saved; and if I do not accept, he would not care if I enter the Fire.'
Then I said to him, 'May I be your ransom! Are you more virtuous, or the Prophets?' He said, 'Rather, the Prophets.'

I said, 'Ya'qub said to Yusuf [12:5]: "O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot a plot against you." Why did he not inform them so that they would not plot against him? Rather he concealed that from them. So likewise did your father conceal from you, for he feared for you.'

He said, 'But by God! If you say that — your companion (the Imam) had already told me in Medina that I would be killed and crucified at al-Kunasa, and that in his possession is a scroll in which is written my killing and my crucifixion.'

Then I performed Hajj and narrated to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) the words of Zayd and what I had said to him. So he said to me: 'You took him from in front of him and from behind him, and from his right and from his left, and from above his head and from beneath his feet, and you left him no path to travel.'

key_terms.الْأَحْوَل: Al-Ahwal ('the cross-eyed'); epithet of Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Nu'man, known as Mu'min al-Taq or Shaitan al-Taq
key_terms.الْكُنَاسَة: Al-Kunasa: a marketplace/place in Kufa where Zayd was indeed killed and crucified
key_terms.حُجَّة: Divine Authority; the Proof of God — the Imam appointed by God on earth
key_terms.صَحِيفَة: A scroll or written document; referring here to the Imam's foreknowledge of future events

ai.seo_question: What did al-Ahwal say to Zayd ibn Ali about the necessity of the Imam as Divine Authority?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates a theological debate between al-Ahwal (Mu'min al-Taq), a close companion of Imam al-Sadiq (AS), and Zayd ibn Ali, a grandson of Imam al-Husayn (AS) who led an armed revolt against the Umayyads. The central argument al-Ahwal makes is that the existence of a divinely-appointed Imam (Hujja) on earth is decisive: if there is one, going with Zayd would lead to destruction since it is unauthorized; if there is none, the question is irrelevant. Imam al-Sadiq's approving response — that al-Ahwal 'left Zayd no path to travel' — validates this reasoning as the authoritative Shia position on the necessity of the Imam and obedience to him, set against the backdrop of Zayd's uprising and his eventual martyrdom at al-Kunasa.
